observations.label: brief-active
observations.output: Cache invalidation is the process of marking stored data as outdated so the system fetches fresh information from the source. Think of it like clearing a sticky note with old directions so you check the map again for your current location. This prevents users from seeing stale or incorrect data when the underlying source changes.

observations.label: detailed-active
observations.output:
Caching saves frequently used data in a fast location so your application doesn't have to fetch it again. However, if the original source changes, that cached copy becomes "stale." Cache invalidation is the process of removing or marking that old data so the next request retrieves the fresh version from the source.

Common strategies include time-to-live (TTL), where the cache automatically expires after a set duration, and versioning, where a change bumps a version number to signal that old copies are obsolete. Developers choose between aggressive purging for consistency and lazy expiration for performance.

Consider the synthetic project Silver Meadow, which serves garden inventory data. When a new plant is added to the database, the system updates a global revision counter. The cache layer detects this new revision and discards the previous inventory list, ensuring the next user sees the accurate, up-to-date stock.
